name: Fosgonimeton
lead: Fosgonimeton (also ATH-1017 or NDX-1017) is an investigational small molecule developed by Athira Pharma as a phosphate prodrug of dihexa, a compound reported to enhance signaling of hepatocyte growth factor (HGF) at its MET receptor.[1][2] It was developed to treat Alzheimer's disease and other dementias, not for any cosmetic purpose, and no study has measured an appearance outcome.

In looksmaxxing and longevity-minded circles the name appears mainly as a relative of dihexa, a nootropic-category research compound. The interest attached to it is cognitive and neurotrophic (brain health) rather than visual, and fosgonimeton itself is not a consumer product.[13]

Human data come from a phase I trial in healthy volunteers and people with Alzheimer's disease, a radiolabelled absorption study, and the phase 2/3 LIFT-AD trial in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease, which was reported not to meet its primary or secondary endpoints.[3][5][9] Most of the rest of the literature is preclinical.[2][7][8]

paras: Fosgonimeton is a prodrug: after administration it is converted to its active metabolite, dihexa, which binds hepatocyte growth factor and is described as potentiating HGF activity at the c-Met receptor.[1][13] The HGF/MET system is a neurotrophic signaling pathway, and the developers proposed that positively modulating it could support neuron health and synaptic connectivity in dementia.[2][4]

Preclinical papers describe neurotrophic and procognitive effects in cell and animal models of dementia.[2] Later laboratory work reported that fosgonimeton reduced amyloid-beta toxicity in primary neuron cultures and models of Alzheimer's disease, including effects on autophagy, and compared its neuroprotective effects with amyloid-targeting antibodies in culture.[7][8][14]

Dihexa (code PNB-0408) is an angiotensin IV-derived oligopeptide that originated in the laboratory of Joseph Harding at Washington State University; the company M3 Biotechnology was founded to commercialize it.[13] That company was renamed Athira Pharma in April 2019, is based in Seattle, and has described fosgonimeton (ATH-1017) as its lead candidate in Alzheimer's disease.[12]

Athira's first president and chief executive, Leen Kawas, resigned in October 2021 after an independent special committee found she had altered images in scientific papers she authored, and the company later paid a reported $4 million settlement in 2025 over allegations related to a federal grant.[12] Reviews of emerging therapies listed fosgonimeton alongside other small molecules in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's disease cognitive impairment and Lewy body dementia pipelines.[10][11][15]

A randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase I trial (NCT03298672) gave daily subcutaneous fosgonimeton to 88 participants across single-ascending-dose (healthy young men), multiple-ascending-dose (healthy older adults, 9 days) and fixed-dose (people with Alzheimer's, 9 days) cohorts. The authors reported that it was safe and well tolerated and that EEG and event-related potential measures supported brain penetration and target engagement.[3]

A phase I absorption, metabolism and excretion study with radiolabelled drug enrolled 8 healthy volunteers.[5] LIFT-AD (NCT04488419), a randomized placebo-controlled phase 2/3 trial that began in 2020 and enrolled 554 participants, tested daily subcutaneous fosgonimeton against placebo; its primary analysis (N=287, participants not on cholinesterase inhibitors) compared a global statistical test combining ADAS-Cog11 and ADCS-ADL23 at week 26.[4][9]

The published report states that the trial did not achieve its primary or secondary endpoints, with a between-group difference of -0.08 on the global score (p=0.70).[9] No studies have examined fosgonimeton for appearance, skin, hair or physique outcomes.

Fosgonimeton is the clinical-stage form of dihexa: dihexa itself is classed by Wikipedia among nootropics and designer drugs and is described there mainly through animal cognitive findings, with no human trial results for dihexa on its own.[13] The prodrug is the version that has human safety data, from the phase I program and the LIFT-AD trial.[3][9]

Fosgonimeton is not approved by any regulator and is not marketed. Review articles on emerging treatments for Parkinson's disease, Lewy body dementia and Alzheimer's disease list it among investigational agents.[10][11][15]

timeline.event: M3 Biotechnology is renamed Athira Pharma.[12]
The LIFT-AD phase 2/3 trial in mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's disease begins (NCT04488419).[4][9]
Athira's founding chief executive resigns following an independent committee finding on altered images.[12]
Phase I safety, tolerability and pharmacokinetic results are published, and a radiolabelled absorption study begins.[3][5]
LIFT-AD results are published, reporting that primary and secondary endpoints were not met.[9]

card.summary: Investigational Alzheimer's drug (a dihexa prodrug) with no appearance data.

quick.overview:
Fosgonimeton is an investigational drug from Athira Pharma that was tested for Alzheimer's disease. It is described as a prodrug of dihexa that boosts HGF/MET signaling.

It has no studied role in appearance. It is a related name in research-compound discussions.
quick.mechanism: It is described as a positive modulator of the HGF/MET neurotrophic pathway, reported in preclinical studies to promote neuronal health and cognition-related effects.
quick.risks: It is not approved for any use. A phase I trial reported on safety and tolerability in volunteers and Alzheimer's patients; details of later-phase results are in the primary literature.
